title: Two Sum
statement: Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`. Exactly one solution exists and you may not use the same element twice. Implement `two_sum(nums, target)`.
hints: Think about what you need to find for each number x, if the target is fixed.
A brute force is O(n^2). What data structure lets you check 'have I seen target - x' in O(1)?
Use a hash map from value to index while scanning left to right.
follow_ups: What is the time and space complexity of your approach?
What if the array is already sorted? Can you use O(1) extra space?

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string `s` of brackets ()[]{}, return True if it is valid: every opener is closed by the same type, in the correct order. Implement `is_valid(s)`.
hints: The most recent unclosed opener must be closed first.
Which data structure gives last-in-first-out?
Push openers; on a closer, pop and compare. At the end the stack must be empty.
follow_ups: What happens for an empty string or a string with only closers?
How would you extend it to also return the index of the first invalid bracket?

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement: `prices[i]` is a stock price on day i. Buy once and sell once later to maximise profit. Return the max profit, or 0 if no profit is possible. Implement `max_profit(prices)`.
hints: For each day, what is the best day to have bought before it?
Track the minimum price seen so far.
Profit on day i = prices[i] - min_so_far; keep the maximum.
follow_ups: What if you can make unlimited transactions?
What does your code return for an empty list?

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. Implement `length_of_longest_substring(s)`.
hints: Brute force checks all substrings. Can you reuse work between neighbouring substrings?
Maintain a window [start, i] that always has unique characters.
When you see a repeated char inside the window, move `start` just past its previous index.
follow_ups: Why is this O(n) even though there is a window shrink step?
What changes if the alphabet is only lowercase letters?

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: Given a non-empty list of integers `nums`, return the largest sum of any contiguous subarray. Implement `max_subarray(nums)`.
hints: At each index, you either extend the previous subarray or start fresh.
Define best_ending_here[i] in terms of best_ending_here[i-1].
cur = max(x, cur + x); answer = max over all cur. Careful with all-negative input.
follow_ups: Can you reduce space to O(1)?
How would you also return the start and end indices?

title: Binary Search
statement: Given a sorted list `nums` and an integer `target`, return the index of `target`, or -1 if absent. Implement `search(nums, target)` in O(log n).
hints: Each comparison should discard half of the remaining range.
Keep two pointers lo and hi, and look at the middle element.
Watch the loop condition (lo <= hi) and the mid +/- 1 updates to avoid infinite loops.
follow_ups: Why can (lo + hi) // 2 overflow in some languages, and how do you avoid it?
How would you find the first occurrence if duplicates exist?

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You climb a staircase of `n` steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top. Implement `climb_stairs(n)`.
hints: Think about the last move you made to reach step n.
ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
You only need the previous two values, so O(1) space is possible.
follow_ups: What is the complexity of the plain recursive version, and how does memoization fix it?
How would the recurrence change if you could also take 3 steps?

title: Coin Change
statement: Given coin denominations `coins` and a target `amount`, return the fewest coins needed to make the amount, or -1 if impossible. Implement `coin_change(coins, amount)`.
hints: Greedy (always pick the largest coin) fails for some inputs. Can you find one?
Let dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a.
dp[a] = min(dp[a - c] + 1) over coins c <= a. Initialise unreachable states with infinity.
follow_ups: What is the time and space complexity in terms of amount and number of coins?
How would you count the number of combinations instead of the minimum coins?

title: Contains Duplicate
statement: Given a list of integers `nums`, return True if any value appears at least twice, else False. Implement `contains_duplicate(nums)`.
hints: Sorting would make duplicates adjacent. What is the cost of that?
A set remembers what you have already seen.
Compare the length of the set with the length of the list, or exit early on the first repeat.
follow_ups: What is the trade-off between the sort approach and the hash set approach?
How would you handle a stream that does not fit in memory?

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given a list `nums`, return a list `out` where out[i] is the product of all elements except nums[i], without using division, in O(n). Implement `product_except_self(nums)`.
hints: out[i] = (product of everything to the left) * (product of everything to the right).
Can you build the left products in one pass?
Do a second pass from the right, multiplying by a running right product, to keep O(1) extra space.
follow_ups: Why is division a problem when the array contains zeros?
What is the extra space if the output array is not counted?
